#10456. 10 Best AI App Builders I've Used in 2026 (and What Each One Gets Wrong)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real users can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

Glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

v0's Free plan gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter plan is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human users.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

#10455. Google Pixel officially re-releases App Lock in beta, Samsung Galaxy gets it too

It’s been a wild ride for Google Pixel’s App Lock feature, but the company is officially re-releasing the feature today, right alongside its debut on Samsung Galaxy devices.

The feature is still only in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 3 for Google Pixel devices, an update that should be released to the stable track in early 2027.

Pixel owners on stable Android 17 QPR2 should already have this! Why would Google make Pixel owners wait until March 2027 to get this?! Release it now to Pixel owners. 🤨

You can still access App Lock by long-pressing on an app icon and adding it to the app lock list.

In a post on Reddit, Google’s Community Engagement Manager details that App Lock on Google Pixel was removed for improvements before getting a full release:

…the product team decided to temporarily pull back the feature from the QPR2 Beta to allow for additional polish, thorough testing, and robust integration across all system surfaces.

That’s why Samsung’s One UI 9.5 beta release today also brings support for App Lock. The feature is built into Android 17 QPR2, seemingly the release that One UI 9.5 is based on, but Google Pixel devices aren’t getting it until QPR3. As far as release timelines go, this means that Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series will probably ship with this feature out of the box, where Pixel phones won’t get it until around March or so. One UI 9.5 won’t roll out for older Galaxy devices until May, if One UI 8.5 serves as an example.

"I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering, a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge wrote in a paper this week, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis."

As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined. "The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation ζ(s) = 0 lie on a certain vertical straight line," the Clay Mathematics Institute explains. "This has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions. A proof that it is true for every interesting solution would shed light on many of the mysteries surrounding the distribution of prime numbers."

As Scientific American notes, the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it.

Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.

This would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy.

Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

"In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds.

Motorola has kicked off its Android 17 rollout for the Razr Fold, marking the first major update for the company’s first book-style foldable, and the start of a potentially interest 7 years of software support.

The Motorola Razr Fold launched with Android 16 back in May 2026, and it remains a really good option for those looking to pick up a book-style foldable in the US. On top of solid specs across the board, it also carries the promise of 7 years of software support, something that few other Moto devices can tout.

#10451. RTO means women risk doing the office housework all over again

Women have already been disproportionately affected by return-to-office mandates, being expected to juggle work, childcare, household responsibilities, and doing the mental gymnastics to stay on top of it all. Now, old-fashioned assumptions about the unpaid work women are expected to take on in the office risk adding to that burden.

Usually, the conversation about mental load centers on household chores, such as who is responsible for doing the laundry, planning meals, and buying the groceries. And it’s women who are more likely to do more domestic labor even when both partners are employed full time. One 2024 study of 3,000 US parents found that mothers took primary responsibility for 71% of household tasks requiring mental effort, compared with 45% for fathers. 

It happens at work, too, where it’s known as “office housework.” These are the unpaid, often unrecognized tasks that keep an organization running but rarely help the people doing them advance their careers. Women therefore can end up doing more work without getting any credit for it.

And RTO might be making things worse.

A study of 1,091 professional women in the US found that 31% reported experiencing everyday gender discrimination when working on-site, compared with 17% when working remotely. This included performing tasks that weren’t their responsibility. The results suggest that being physically present can expose women to more everyday gender discrimination and create more opportunities for these assumptions to surface.

The problem is also evident in the UK. In a new survey of 2,000 working women and men by advocacy group Co-operatives UK, 22% of women said they’d been asked to do paperwork outside their role, 21% had been asked to clean or tidy the office, and 20% had been asked to make coffee for senior leaders. Overall, nearly half (49%) of women said they’d been asked more than once to do something outside their role, such as making tea or booking a meeting room.

Women have been highlighting the problem on social media, sharing their experiences and how they push back against the assumption that they’ll take on these tasks.

One content creator, Alex Schudy, said she had noticed colleagues using what she described as “weaponized incompetence” to try to get her to take notes in meetings, often by throwing her a compliment to disguise it. In her video on TikTok, she said she let the “silence linger” when one colleague suggested she do it because her handwriting was neat and she was “organized.” She politely declined, explaining that she needed to focus on presenting her part of the meeting. Someone else was designated the notetaker instead.

Another creator, Anna Kennedy, described in a video how much office housework she had come to realise women were doing — from keeping track of action items and chasing colleagues to making sure feedback was acted upon.

“Things that keep the machine moving fundamentally, but are not rewarded or seen in a performance review,” she said. “I’m never, I swear to God, never seeing men doing this kind of work.”

As more employees settle back into office life, many hope there have been changes for the better, particularly around work-life balance and flexibility. But some of the oldest workplace habits seem stubbornly resistant to change, and it’s time women stopped being expected to pick up the slack. 

Ultimately, they shouldn’t have to spend their working days doing the jobs that keep everyone else organized, only to be left behind as everyone else speeds ahead.

#10449. The future of live entertainment

Change is in the air. Digital saturation is reshaping nearly every dimension of our lives in this age of artificiality, transforming how we work, communicate, and experience the world around us.

Amid this profound transformation, our desire for experiences that are deeply human has never been greater.

Technology can do so much, including simulating interaction and placing nearly limitless entertainment at our fingertips. But it cannot fully replicate formative live entertainment moments like the collective anticipation before a performance or the emotional release of thousands of people experiencing the same unforgettable moment together.

Human beings are fundamentally social. We are drawn to one another and transformed by shared experience. Gathering is part of who we are. That fundamental human desire places us on the precipice of a cultural renaissance.

Throughout history, moments of mass disruption have repeatedly created the conditions for extraordinary periods of advancement in art, science, architecture, technology, and design. These moments force societies to question familiar assumptions and search for new ways to understand one another.

We are entering such a moment now.

In this emerging age of artificiality, human creativity will command a new premium. So will presence. The experiences we cannot download, automate, or predict will become more valuable precisely because they are real.

For designers (and any type of creative), this is an extraordinary opportunity. We have the ability—and responsibility—to shape the experiences that define the next era of culture.

4 IDEAS TO GUIDE THE NEXT ERA OF CULTURE

History demonstrates that people are remarkably resilient. When confronted with uncertainty or moments of radical change, we search for reasons to believe in what comes next, then adapt accordingly. What follows are four ideas that can help ensure this latest cultural renaissance is a period of meaningful transformation that unites people globally for a shared purpose: connection.

1. The importance of optimism 

That instinct remains powerful today. According to recent research from VML Intelligence, 69% of respondents regularly feel hopeful about the future. Beneath the anxiety surrounding technological and cultural change, optimism persists.

That optimism matters because hope rarely remains an individual emotion. People seek opportunities to express it collectively. Live entertainment gives physical form to that desire.

Watching Lionel Messi with his foot on the ball in the 90th minute of the FIFA World Cup, a stadium erupting in victory, a concert audience singing a chorus with Taylor Swift, or a theater falling completely silent at the same emotional moment reveals something profound. Emotion becomes amplified when it’s shared.

The most successful venues build anticipation and entice participation. They create the conditions for strangers to feel connected.

As optimism becomes a defining force in the next cultural era, the places that bring people together will become increasingly important expressions of collective possibility.

2. The return of real

The renewed interest in analog experiences is already visible across culture. Vinyl records, tapes, and physical media have returned to prominence. Film cameras and Polaroids are reappearing at concerts and celebrations. Tactile pursuits such as journaling and knitting are attracting new generations.

These behaviors are sometimes dismissed as nostalgia. But they represent something more consequential: a desire for agency and authenticity. It is a tangible connection in a world of infinite, algorithmically delivered content.

People want experiences they can touch and remember. They want the imperfect and the unpredictable. They desire the unrepeatable. Live entertainment is the ultimate expression of that desire.

No two performances are the same. No crowd produces the same energy. No professional athlete reacts in the same way in that critical winning moment. The possibility that something unexpected might happen is the source of its power.

Designers are beginning to respond through spaces that encourage deeper presence and participation. Listening rooms, intimate performance spaces, flexible venues, and carefully choreographed social environments are creating new ways to experience music and culture together.

In the age of artificiality, the real becomes rare. Rarity creates the ultimate value.

3. From experience to transformation

This cultural recalibration aligns with B. Joseph Pine’s concept of the transformation economy. This is the idea that people increasingly seek experiences that change them.

Businesses and institutions will increasingly be judged by what they provide and by whether the experiences they create feel meaningful and transformative. This is especially true in sports and live entertainment, where identity, ritual, and emotion are inseparable from the event itself.

The 2026 FIFA World Cup offered a powerful expression of this idea. Supporters traveled from across the globe not simply to watch soccer, but to participate in one of humanity’s great, shared traditions. The matches mattered, but so did the pilgrimage, the gathering, the rituals, and the sense of belonging to a global community.

The same principle exists at every scale, spanning the intimacy of a listening room to the collective roar of a stadium and everything in between. Each can become a place where human connection is forged, moments that become treasured memories.

4. A collective opportunity awaits

The next era of live entertainment will be defined by how thoughtfully technology is used to deepen, not displace, the human experience.

Our greatest opportunity is to design places that encourage people to look up from their devices, toward the performance and toward one another. Places that transform attendance into participation, audiences into communities, and fleeting moments into enduring memories.

These places give physical form to the things artificial intelligence cannot manufacture; chief among them, authentic, spontaneous, and shared emotion.

The conditions for a cultural renaissance are already here. Its character, however, is not predetermined. It will be shaped by the choices of many, including cultural and entertainment leaders. Let’s collectively embrace an opportunity to design and lead a new era. It’s one that doesn’t come often and can spark lasting impacts that will positively influence generations to come.

Brian Mirakian is senior principal at Populous.

#10445. People are using Meta’s Muse to purge who they’re following on Instagram

Since the days of MySpace’s Top 8, social media has made it easy to hurt your friends’ feelings. Some platforms make it easy to judge relative friendship, like Snapchat’s publicly viewable “Best Friends” feature.

Instagram, however, keeps users’ social dynamics under wraps from one another, with accounts unable to see when someone unfollows them. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has previously said the platform hasn’t introduced a “who unfollowed me” feature so that users feel free to unfollow whomever they please without fear of judgment or tension.

But a new tool from Instagram’s parent company Meta is shaking things up. Its AI assistant Muse has an apparently petty personality under its cute and cuddly exterior—and it’s happy to help users spot who isn’t following them back and then unfollow them en masse.

How Muse can purge your Instagram

Social media users have discovered that Muse can sort through the people they follow on Instagram and point out any non-mutual connections. Though third-party apps have offered similar features in the past, they’re notorious for getting accounts flagged and taken down from Instagram. Muse, as an in-house app, doesn’t pose the same risk.

One Instagram user who tried out the feature, Khalil Roberts, told Wired about his experience using Muse. Roberts gave Muse the prompt, “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on Instagram, and can you unfollow them for me.” It quickly returned an Excel spreadsheet with 151 accounts that fit his criteria, then asked if he wanted to follow through on unfollowing them.

Roberts was among the chorus on social media singing Muse’s praises for letting them purge such accounts so easily. “I just cleared 80+ chopped hos who thought I was a fan,” one user posted.

“Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG,” another user boasted, crediting Muse in a follow-up post.

Meta’s secret menu

Though Muse’s potential for pettiness is a much-requested feature, it’s only being spread through word of mouth. Meta itself isn’t advertising the capability—or at least not anymore.

In October, Los Angeles-based social media consultant Rachel Karten noticed a Meta ad on Instagram touting that Muse could let users “see who unfollowed you each week.”

“I get that this is technically a requested feature but wouldn’t it lead to more resentment towards your own platform?” Karten asked in a post sharing a screenshot of the ad.

Indeed, Instagram has since taken down the ad, as a Meta representative confirmed to Business Insider. Still, the feature remains active in Muse—as long as users know to ask for it.

#10443. Top 6 AI Detector Tools in 2026: Features, Accuracy Claims and When to Trust Them

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

• A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

• Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

Limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and says other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page says false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

• Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

OpenAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

• Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and update as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control

group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical"

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function."""

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0})

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan")

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan")

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}")

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

• Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

Yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

The top scorer of South Korea's Certified Tax Accountant exam confessed to AI-assisted cheating, prompting the South Korean government to tighten anti-cheating measures for its incredibly important CSAT exams.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

South Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices. The anti-cheating measure was announced after a cheater in South Korea’s tax accountant exam confessed to using AI and a micro-camera to cheat. The alerts caught a total of 54 candidates, with 111 total when combined with other means, The Korean Herald reports.

The College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most important yearly events. The exam is so significant that the whole country pauses and makes way for the test-takers; police clear the roads and escort late students, noisy construction and maintenance are suspended, aircraft are grounded, military exercises are paused, and the stock market opens an hour later. The government even requests public institutions and private companies start work later, delaying the rush hour and ensuring the students arrive unimpeded.

The brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives. With such high stakes, cheating is not unusual.

The month before the CSAT, South Korea’s Certified Tax Accountant exam received an unusually large number of high scorers — with 66 candidates scoring over 90+ in introductory accounting over only two in 2025 and one in 2024, as reported by The Korean Herald. The top scorer, Han Won-seok, confessed to cheating on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, admitting to cheating using a micro-camera that feeds images of the test to an AI on his smartphone.

The confession went live days before the Suneung, prompting the South Korean government to tighten up its anti-cheating measures for the exam, with Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung stating, "Cheating involving the abuse of AI in South Korea, where public examinations significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources, rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust," calling for an overhaul of the system to address AI-assisted cheating, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

The first alert rang at 8:30 AM, ten minutes before the exam started, catching 31 students with unauthorized devices, whose scores were immediately invalidated despite the test not having started yet. The next two alerts at 2:21 and 2:57 PM caught 23 more, bringing the total to 54. As of today, Yonhap News Agency reports that 111 total students were caught with unauthorized devices — 52 were caught through other methods such as metal detectors, WiFi signal detection, and physical inspections, with a further five caught red-handed using prohibited devices.

Alongside the South Korean government’s reaction to the confession, a law school entrance exam candidate accused of AI-assisted cheating like Han Won-seok had died on the day of the Suneung. In July, Lee Jin-woo, a Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) candidate, achieved an impressive perfect score and is reportedly the first to do so. Months later, he published a book about his study methods, talking about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and even reduced smartphone use.

When the tax accountant cheater confessed on Sunday, it led to online suspicion about Lee’s perfect LEET score, with two lawyers even filing legal complaints accusing him of obstruction of official duties. Lee was supposed to be interviewed on YouTube early on Thursday to prove his academic abilities, but he did not show up. Later that day, when Police investigated the legal complaints and after he was reported missing, he was found dead of cardiac arrest at 1:12 PM in a motel, with a note at the scene stating he was mentally and physically exhausted, with no mention of the cheating allegations, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

#10440. America’s next quantum breakthrough: The factory floor

Building a quantum computing company has taught me something that wasn’t always obvious to me as a scientist. Developing a new technology is one challenge. Figuring out how to manufacture it reliably, at scale, is another. And the second can be every bit as difficult as the first.

For years, the prevailing wisdom in technology was to focus on what you do best and outsource the rest. It made good business sense. Building manufacturing capacity is expensive, complicated, and often far removed from the work that inspired someone to start a technology company in the first place.

But that approach comes with a tradeoff. When you depend on someone else to manufacture your technology, you also depend on their capabilities, priorities, and timelines.

For an emerging industry like quantum information, those dependencies can become significant obstacles. And I believe they have implications well beyond any one company.

A LESSON WE’VE ALREADY LEARNED

The United States has seen what happens when technological innovation and manufacturing become separated.

American companies designed many of the advanced semiconductors powering today’s AI revolution, but much of the manufacturing capacity needed to produce them was developed overseas. That arrangement supported decades of innovation and economic growth. It also created dependencies that have become increasingly difficult to ignore.

Now, the U.S. is investing heavily in rebuilding domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity. It’s a difficult and expensive undertaking, and one that will take years to fully realize.

Quantum technologies give us an opportunity to think about these challenges earlier in an industry’s development.

The U.S. has extraordinary strengths in quantum science. Our universities, national laboratories, and private companies have helped advance the field for decades. But the path from a scientific breakthrough to a useful product requires more than research. Much more. It requires specialized materials, fabrication processes, engineering expertise, and the ability to produce increasingly complex technologies consistently and economically.

Those capabilities need to develop alongside science.

WHY WE CHOSE TO BUILD

I’ve experienced this challenge firsthand at Quantum Computing Inc. Our work in quantum photonics depends on highly specialized manufacturing processes. As we developed our technology, we had to think carefully about how much of our future we wanted to depend on outside manufacturing partners.

For a growing company, investing in your own manufacturing capabilities is a consequential decision. It requires capital, specialized expertise, and a willingness to take on responsibilities that extend well beyond research and product development.

We ultimately decided to build and acquire manufacturing capacity because we believe greater control over the critical and proprietary processes is essential to our long-term strategy. For other processes, we will leverage existing manufacturing capabilities and collaborate with industry partners to build a robust, reliable, and sustainable supply chain. 

We also see an opportunity to contribute to the broader ecosystem by making our manufacturing capabilities available to others. The quantum opportunity is far bigger than any one company.  Advancing the industry will require collaboration and shared capabilities that benefit all of us. It’s time to work together to build that foundation and accelerate the growth of the quantum industry.

NO ONE MANUFACTURING MODEL

That decision has shaped how I think about innovation.

When researchers and engineers have closer access to manufacturing, they can learn from what happens during fabrication and use that knowledge to improve the next design. Manufacturing becomes part of the development process itself. The experience gained along the way can be just as valuable as the equipment.

There is no single manufacturing model that makes sense for every quantum company. Different technologies have different requirements, and outside foundries and specialized partners remain important. But access to reliable manufacturing capacity can have a profound influence on how quickly an idea becomes something useful.

BUILD AN INDUSTRY, NOT JUST A TECHNOLOGY

Washington D.C. is beginning to recognize this challenge. A June executive order addressing quantum technology calls for strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities and expanding partnerships between government and private industry.

I welcome that attention. But building a manufacturing base requires more than funding announcements and policy commitments. It takes facilities, equipment, specialized talent, and years of experience developing processes that work consistently. It also requires demand from companies that are ready to move technologies out of the laboratory and into practical use.

Other countries recognize the importance of these capabilities, with many having committed substantial resources to quantum technology. The United States has important advantages in research, entrepreneurship, and private investment. We should be building on those strengths now.

That doesn’t mean every component needs to be manufactured domestically. International partnerships and global supply chains will continue to play important roles. But we should be deliberate about which capabilities are essential to our technological independence, making sure we have the capacity to develop and sustain them.

FINAL THOUGHTS

I’ve spent much of my career working to advance quantum technology. Like many scientists, I was initially drawn to the possibilities of what we could discover and what those discoveries make possible.

Today, I spend just as much time thinking about what it takes to turn those possibilities into something people can use. That means manufacturing, supply chains, engineering, and all the difficult work that follows a breakthrough.

The U.S. has an extraordinary foundation in quantum science. What we do with that advantage now matters. We need to invest in the ability to manufacture these technologies with the same conviction and intensity we brought to discovering them.

Yuping Huang is CEO of Quantum Computing Inc.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

Not sure if you’ve heard, but the biggest video game of all time is out today: buying Anthropic stock. Yes, in case you haven’t already blown all of your money on the GTA VI Ultimate Edition, you can try your luck at buying one of the most anticipated IPOs of all time when ANT goes public on the Nasdaq later today.

But you’re likely up, playing the game that is, according to Metacritic, already among the best of all time. It’s currently sitting at a near-perfect 99/100 on the aggregator, with reviewers calling it “a masterpiece” and “gaming’s… greatest love story.” It’s a game in which you can do basically anything you want, from the violent to the vacuous.

More than anything, though, I’m just excited to discover all the different ways the game allows you to find and consume coffee.

As I’m sure happened in every newsroom, the conversation this week turned to whether traffic will meaningfully decline today as up to 1.5 million people “call in sick” to play GTA VI. If you’ve been awake since the crack of dawn trying to meander your way to Vice City, you’re just one of many folks experiencing the rarest of moments in 2026: a singular, unifying cultural event.

My biggest question isn’t whether gamers will play GTA VI but whether normies will. Previous games in the series, particularly GTA V, sold hundreds of millions of copies and still draw countless players today. GTA VI feels even more inviting to those who just want to spend time in its sandbox to do some fishing, dancing, or flying. One reviewer even called it a “cozy game” where he just spent time walking around a zoo.

While the size, scale, and impact of GTA VI are exponentially higher, the last time I heard people talking about a game in this way was during the pandemic, when everyone was hunkering down for a winter of Animal Crossing.

By the way, GTA VI has a functioning smartphone that can be used for making calls, sending texts, taking photos, looking at “Instagram,” and setting reminders, among other things. It’s yet another minor detail in a game full of them. Plus, it looks like an original Pixel.

#10437. The poster for the Sam Altman movie looks like AI slop. It’s actually brilliant marketing

The official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands.

Anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes. So when film studio Neon released the poster this week, users on social media were quick to catch oddities in the illustration, leading some to suspect it was made using AI.

At first glance, the poster looks normal.

On a closer look, Andrew Garfield, who plays Sam Altman in the movie, doesn’t appear quite like himself, lingering somewhere in the uncanny valley. The background features San Francisco’s landscape, except the Golden Gate Bridge is underwater. The tree behind Garfield looks distorted, with a Pinocchio-like face surfacing from the trunk. The branches are no less strange, morphing into snakes.

The closer you look, the weirder it gets.

Just a few hours after the poster was rolled out on social media, Neon followed up with a video showing a human drawing the scene by hand, crediting illustrator Mike Thompson and creative studio Gravillis.

“Art made by humans,” Neon captioned the behind-the-scenes video on X.

Users on social media quickly changed their tune, praising the studio and the movie’s creative team for their approach to the poster design.

“The poster for [Artificial] being made by an actual human artist while made to look like it was AI generated wow that’s luca GODagnino,” one user said on X.

Another user added, “This poster is a masterpiece. So many fun, completely bizarre, and purposeful ‘AI Slop’ touches. Zoom in and see if you can spot them all.”

Many also took notice that Neon didn’t just come out and say the poster was made by humans but rather made the effort to film a behind-the-scenes video and upload it as proof.

“Thank you for filming their processes and including the views of the artists in a world where what we see can be compromised or untrue,” one user said on X.

People-powered

Neon is not the first company to show how its work was made as a way to stand apart from AI slop. In recent months, brands across retail and tech have done the same.

In August, Apple released a behind-the-scenes video of its claymation ad for the new Mac Mini. Prada’s animated holiday campaign includes sketches from the artist.

But behind-the-scenes footage works only when the ads themselves are craft-forward, leaning on labor-intensive handwork as a form of effort signaling.

While proof of humanness taps into the film’s theme—bringing a sense of irony by making human art look artificial—not every observer is embracing the marketing trend.

One X user proclaimed, “Anybody posting any type of art now has to prove to morons that it was genuinely created by them and not AI. What a shit hole time period we live in.”

#10435. AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

It has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry-level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs—there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. 

The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences.

The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers). 

That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers, in particular, dominate six jobs that are likely to see the biggest decline in labor demand, according to McKinsey, including postal mail carriers and customer service representatives; Latino workers are also especially likely to hold some of those jobs, namely dishwashers and hand packers. 

Black and Latino workers—along with workers in rural regions—are also much more likely to be in jobs that involve physical labor, which are more vulnerable to being automated through robotics and other AI-enabled systems.

On the whole, lower-wage workers will face the greatest impact, and are 7.6 times as likely to need to transition into a new job when compared to higher-wage workers; people without a college degree are 1.8 times more likely to need to do the same. 

Meanwhile, white workers are better positioned to both avoid this level of AI disruption and actually benefit from AI adoption in a number of ways. It’s not just that they’re more likely to hold jobs where AI will enhance their work, boosting productivity rather than replacing employees outright. When compared to their Black and Latino counterparts, white workers are also 30% to 50% more likely to work in the industries where private capital will be deployed, yielding more jobs and wealth creation, the McKinsey report states. 

That means white workers already have more of a foothold in jobs involving robotics or semiconductors or biotech, setting them up for success as hundreds of billions of dollars pour into those industries. (Look no further than the Anthropic IPO this week, which has created thousands of millionaires.) 

In other words: Without broader policy changes or reskilling initiatives, many Black and Latino workers may be forced out of their jobs and locked out of opportunities to cash in on the AI boom.

#10431. ‘The Hunger Games’ are back: Haymitch Abernathy can teach the C-suite about reluctant leadership

Around the office today, you might hear: “May the odds be ever in your favor.” After the tumultuous technical failures of the past week, the phrase might come off as alarming, but it’s actually a Hunger Games reference.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters today and tells Haymitch Abernathy’s origin story. Abernathy is an unlikely hero forced into leadership in the rebellion by circumstances out of his control.

This doesn’t mean the C-suite can’t learn a thing or two from him. Here are a few quick stats on the franchise and some of Haymitch’s best management lessons.

The Hunger Games franchise by the numbers

The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, the first book in the original trilogy, was published by Scholastic on September 14, 2008. It was followed by Catching Fire in 2009 and Mockingjay in 2010.

Before the second book even came out, Lionsgate acquired the film rights for the first book. It was a smart move because the four Hunger Games films have collectively made more than $1.45 billion at the domestic box office.

Collins took a break after the first trilogy. A stand-alone prequel novel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, came out in 2020, telling the backstory of Coriolanus Snow. The 2023 film version made more than $166 million at the domestic box office.

Sunrise on the Reaping was published in 2025. According to Deadline, the new film is expected to make at least $80 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend alone.

Haymitch Abernathy: Reluctant leader archetype

Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in Sunrise, is an unconventional leader. He would rather be drinking away his sorrows than changing the fate of Panem—but sometimes management is thrust upon us.

Abernathy excels at strategic planning. In the original books and movies, he is able to guide Peeta and Katniss through the games two times while organizing a rebellion right under the Capitol’s nose. This comes through very careful planning and deception.

In the real world, however, business leaders need to be able to communicate a clear vision and how to execute it.

Abernathy is rough around the edges—and his tough exterior allows him to work with a diverse range of difficult colleagues to get results. You could call him a people-first strategist. For instance, he was able to get through to Katniss and help her play the public relations game by pretending to have feelings for Peeta. She did that so well that her love for him ended up becoming real.

In addition, Abernathy got the vain people of the Capitol to empathize with Katniss and Peeta and send them lifesaving supplies like medicine and water.

Plan, collaborate, and adapt

Similarly, managers will have to work with many different personalities, departments, or vendors. True leaders can approach each individual or organization in a way that uplifts their strengths.

Back in Panem, all this planning doesn’t mean the reluctant Abernathy can’t adapt. He thrives under pressure. He was the victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell. He had to compete against 47 other tributes, double the usual amount. He won by using the force field around the arena against his opponent.

In business, as in the Hunger Games, not everything is going to go according to the five-year-plan. Sometimes you have to improvise solutions as problems arise.

As it hits theaters, Sunrise will reveal more of Abernathy’s story and administrative prowess. The business world should take note.

#10429. How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

The bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

The first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems.

Maybe you want to express your nuanced opinions at a sporting event. Maybe you want to pick someone up at the airport, complete with the traditional name on a sign.

The problem with posters, however, is you have to make them ahead of time. And carry them. And somehow keep them from crumpling in traffic.

And while it’s true that no digital tool can re-create the charm of something cut, glued, and markered with your own two hands, it’s better than nothing. Because, to borrow an old adage about photography, the best poster is the one you have with you.

This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence. Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures!

Turn any screen into a poster

​Bigwords.page​ is an easy-to-remember website that does one thing:

➜ It turns your screen into an instant, impossible-to-miss poster for easy viewing from any distance. It’ll even keep your device from going to sleep, the way a video does.

Just type your message, choose a font and color scheme, then hit the full-screen button—and your message shows up in crisp, clear letters.

⌚ Setup is instant, and the entire process to create a billboard-like poster will take you at most 60 seconds. Just load the website, click the button to fire up the editor, and then type in whatever you want—with any appearance you like.

Most of the time, you’ll just need to type a message and hit full screen, but you can tweak things a little. You can change the colors, format with Markdown, and choose among a few fonts.

And there are a few handy additional features. You can add a countdown to your poster, if you want. You can add an image. There are animations. You can even add a QR code, which you can use to add a link or a Wi-Fi network. These features make this tool potentially useful at work—you could turn a TV or computer into a temporary billboard at your office or store.

For most people, though, this is a way to quickly turn any phone or tablet into a temporary poster. Give it a shot the next time you want to broadcast a thought, or add a custom message to a photo.

The best part: Because it’s a website, there’s nothing to download and no application you need to install. All you need to do is remember the URL.

  • Bigwords.page runs in any browser​, meaning you can use it on any device.
  • It’s completely free (and even open source if you want to run it on your own server).
  • Your message never leaves your browser—it’s never sent to a server. There are no ads.

#10424. Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle.

When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. 

We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle.

That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question.

Define the bar, then pay against it

When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. 

We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. 

At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. 

The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a new AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. 

Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. 

We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. 

To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the company will keep benefiting from that work every year. 

Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band.

For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group.

Reward your talent for making their expertise reusable

Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge. 

This is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.

The Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless features a black metal top plate, double-shot PBT keycaps with shine-through legends, per-key RGB lighting, Asus' linear ROG NX Snow Switches, sound-dampening foam, a wrist rest, and tri-mode wireless functionality. In our review of the ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless, we gave the board a 4.5-star rating, calling the tenkeyless layout a "perfect compromise between gaming/enthusiast and full-size/compact" keyboards. While you'll find linear switches instead of optical, they're fully lubed out of the box, adding to the overall high-quality out-of-the-box experience you typically only get with more enthusiast-focused keyboards. For those looking to grab a premium mechanical keyboard on the cheap, the ROG Strix Scope II 96 strikes a fine balance between features, size, build quality, and more, offering a cohesive typing and gaming experience that's adaptable to almost any kind of user out there. While Asus' ROG products are often over the top in design, this board is delightfully muted by comparison, and won't look out of place on your desk or in an office. Now hitting an all-time low price point, you're getting a lot for your money here, as the keyboard ships with just about every user out there. For those looking for a smart, no-frills mechanical keyboard this Black Friday, it's hard to go wrong with the ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless.
